The cells oppose each other, so the **net** emf drives the current through **all three**
resistances.
**Step 1 — find the net emf.** Connected in opposition, the smaller emf subtracts:
E_net = **E₁ − E₂** ✓
positive, since E₁ > E₂, so the current circulates in the sense set by E₁.
**Step 2 — find the total resistance.** Both internal resistances and the external
resistance are in series around the single loop:
R_total = **r₁ + r₂ + R** ✓
**Step 3 — find the current.**
I = (E₁ − E₂)/(r₁ + r₂ + R)
**Step 4 — find the terminal potential difference.** It is the voltage across the
external resistance:
V = IR
= **(E₁ − E₂)R/(r₁ + r₂ + R)** ✓
**Why r₂ appears in the denominator even though E₂ opposes.** Internal resistance
**always** adds, whichever way the cell is turned ✓ Only the emf changes sign; the
resistance does not.
**Why the external R must be included.** The current flows through the whole loop, and
Ohm's law applies to the **total** circuit ✓ Two of the four options omit R from the
denominator, and both can be eliminated on that ground alone.
**A dimensional check on those options.** (E₁ − E₂)R/(r₁ + r₂) has units
V x Ω/Ω = **V** ✓ so dimensions alone do not separate them - but physically, leaving R
out of the denominator would make the current independent of the load, which is wrong.
**A worked instance.** E₁ = 6 V, E₂ = 2 V, r₁ = r₂ = 1 Ω, R = 2 Ω:
I = 4/4 = **1 A**
V = 1 x 2 = **2 V** ✓
and a check round the loop: 6 − 1(1) − 2 − 1(1) − 1(2) = **0** ✓ Kirchhoff's loop rule
is satisfied.
**What happens to the weaker cell.** It is being **charged** - the current is driven
backwards through it by the stronger cell ✓ This is exactly how a battery charger works,
and it is why the net emf is the difference.
**Reading the distractors.** The options with **E₁ + E₂** ✗ describe cells connected to
**aid** each other, not in opposition ✓
∴ (E₁ − E₂)R/(r₁ + r₂ + R).

The bridge balances when **P/Q = R/S′**, so find the S′ required and then the shunt that
produces it.
**Step 1 — write the balance condition.**
P/Q = R/S′
2/2 = 2/S′
**S′ = 2 Ω** ✓
So the fourth arm must be reduced from 3 Ω to 2 Ω.
**Step 2 — shunt S with an unknown x.** The parallel combination must equal 2 Ω:
(3x)/(3 + x) = 2
**Step 3 — solve.**
3x = 6 + 2x
**x = 6 Ω** ✓
**Step 4 — verify.**
(3 x 6)/(3 + 6) = 18/9 = **2 Ω** ✓ and then P/Q = 1 = R/S′ ✓ the bridge balances.
**Why a shunt can only reduce.** A parallel resistance is always **smaller** than either
branch ✓ Since S must come down from 3 Ω to 2 Ω, shunting is the right operation; no
shunt could ever raise it.
**How large the shunt must be.** The required reduction is modest - 3 Ω to 2 Ω - so the
shunt is comparatively **large**, 6 Ω ✓ A small shunt would pull the combination far
below 2 Ω: shunting with 1 Ω would give 0·75 Ω.
**The general formula.** To bring S down to a target value S′,
**x = SS′/(S − S′)** ✓
Here (3)(2)/(3 − 2) = **6 Ω** ✓ in one step, and it shows why x grows without limit as
S′ approaches S.
**What balance means.** With P/Q = R/S the two midpoints sit at the **same potential**,
so the galvanometer carries no current ✓ The bridge is then insensitive to the
galvanometer's resistance and to the battery's emf, which is what makes it accurate.
**Reading the distractors.** Testing each in the parallel formula:
1 Ω gives **0·75 Ω** ✗
2 Ω gives **1·2 Ω** ✗
4 Ω gives **1·71 Ω** ✗
Only 6 Ω gives exactly 2 Ω ✓ so substituting the options is a quick route to the answer.
∴ 6 Ω.

To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, add a **series** resistance large enough that
full-scale current flows at the desired voltage.
**Step 1 — write the condition.** At full scale the whole 3 V must drive the full-scale
current through the galvanometer and the series resistance together:
V = I_g(G + R)
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
R = V/I_g − G
**Step 3 — substitute.**
R = 3/(5 x 10⁻⁴) − 50
= 6000 − 50
= **5950 Ω** ✓
**Why the series resistance must be large.** The galvanometer full-scales at only
**0·5 mA**, so to drop 3 V the total resistance must be 6000 Ω ✓ The galvanometer's own
50 Ω is a tiny part of that, and the multiplier supplies the rest.
**Why subtracting G matters here.** It changes 6000 to 5950 - under 1% ✓ but the options
include both, so the question is testing whether the galvanometer's own resistance is
accounted for. In an exam the difference between 5950 and 6000 is the whole mark.
**Why a voltmeter needs a high resistance.** It is connected in **parallel** with the
component being measured, so it must draw as little current as possible ✓ Here the
finished voltmeter has 6000 Ω and draws only 0·5 mA at full scale, disturbing the
circuit very little.
**The sensitivity of this voltmeter.**
6000 Ω ÷ 3 V = **2000 Ω per volt** ✓ the standard way of rating an analogue voltmeter;
a higher figure means a better instrument.
**The contrast with an ammeter.** An ammeter is made by adding a **small shunt in
parallel**, to keep its resistance low ✓ Series multiplier for a voltmeter, parallel
shunt for an ammeter - the two conversions are mirror images.
**Reading the distractors.** **5050 Ω** ✗ and **5059 Ω** ✗ match no step of the
arithmetic. **595 Ω** ✗ is a factor of ten out, from using 5 x 10⁻³ A ✓ Substituting
back - I = 3/(595 + 50) = 4·65 mA, far above full scale - rules it out.
∴ 5950 Ω.

Current density is current **per unit cross-sectional area**.
**Step 1 — find the area of the conductor.** With diameter d = 0·1 mm = 10⁻⁴ m:
A = πd²/4
= 3(10⁻⁴)²/4
= 3 x 10⁻⁸/4
= **7·5 x 10⁻⁹ m²**
**Step 2 — convert the current.**
90 mA = **0·09 A** = 9 x 10⁻² A
**Step 3 — divide.**
J = I/A
= 9 x 10⁻²/(7·5 x 10⁻⁹)
= **1·2 x 10⁷ A m⁻²** ✓
**Why the approximation π ≈ 3 is given.** It makes the arithmetic exact: 3 x 10⁻⁸/4 =
7·5 x 10⁻⁹ ✓ With π = 3·1416 the answer would be 1·15 x 10⁷, which rounds to the same
option.
**A sense of the magnitude.** Over ten million amperes per square metre sounds enormous,
but the wire is extremely fine - only a tenth of a millimetre across ✓ Household wiring
runs at about 10⁶ A m⁻², and a current density of 10⁷ in so thin a wire would heat it
considerably.
**The relation to drift velocity.**
J = n e v_d ✓
With n ≈ 8·5 x 10²⁸ m⁻³ for copper:
v_d = 1·2 x 10⁷/(8·5 x 10²⁸ x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹) = **8·8 x 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹**
under a millimetre per second - the familiar result that electrons drift extremely
slowly even in a heavily loaded wire.
**Why current density matters.** Unlike current, it is a **local** quantity, defined at
each point ✓ It is what determines heating per unit volume and what fixes the
current-carrying capacity of a conductor, whatever its overall size.
**The commonest error.** Using the **diameter** in place of the **radius**, or forgetting
the factor 4 in πd²/4 ✓ That mistake gives 3 x 10⁶ A m⁻² - exactly one of the
distractors.
**Reading the other distractors.** **2·4 x 10⁷** ✗ is twice the answer, and **6 x 10⁶**
✗ half of it ✓
∴ 1.2 × 10⁷.

Resistance grows with **length** and falls with **cross-sectional area**, so the longest
and thinnest wire has the greatest resistance.
**Step 1 — write the resistance.**
R = ρL/A
= ρL/(πd²/4)
= **4ρL/(πd²)** ✓
so
**R ∝ L/d²**
**Step 2 — see what maximises it.** R is largest when L is **as large as possible** and d
**as small as possible** ✓ Length helps directly; thinness helps as the **square**, so
it matters more.
**Step 3 — test the options against L/d².**
L and d: **L/d²** - the baseline
2L and d: 2L/d² = **2 times** the baseline
L/2 and 2d: (L/2)/(4d²) = **1/8** of the baseline
2L and d/2: 2L/(d²/4) = **8 times** the baseline ✓ the largest
**Step 4 — conclude.** **2L and d/2** gives the maximum resistance ✓
**Why halving the diameter counts for so much.** It quarters the **area**, since
A ∝ d² ✓ so the resistance quadruples from that alone, and doubling the length doubles
it again - a factor of eight in all.
**The drawing-out picture.** Stretching a wire makes it longer **and** thinner at once ✓
If the volume is conserved, doubling the length gives L' = 2L with A' = A/2, so
R' = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = **4R** ✓ The general rule for a stretched wire is R ∝ L², and this is
why a drawn-out wire's resistance rises so steeply.
**A note on the options.** Taken literally, "2L and d/2" does not conserve the volume of
copper - that combination holds only half as much metal as "L and d". The question is
asking which of the four **stated** shapes has the greatest resistance, and on the
L/d² measure that is unambiguously 2L and d/2 ✓
**Reading the other distractors.** **L and d** ✗ is the starting shape and maximises
nothing. **2L and d** ✗ gains only a factor of two. **L/2 and 2d** ✗ is the shortest and
thickest - the **minimum** resistance of the four ✓
∴ 2 L and d/2.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, L and d. That is simply the original shape;
since R ∝ L/d², the four options scale as 1, 2, 1/8 and 8 times that value, so 2L and
d/2 gives the maximum. The key has been corrected to the fourth option.

Heating the coil raises its resistance, and the balance point shifts **towards the side
whose resistance has grown**.
**Step 1 — write the balance condition.** With the coil of resistance X in the left gap
and the standard resistance S in the right:
X/S = ℓ/(100 − ℓ) ✓
**Step 2 — see what heating does to the coil.** The coil is metallic, and the resistance
of a metal **increases** with temperature:
R_t = R₀(1 + αΔt), with α positive ✓
So X **increases** when the water is heated.
**Step 3 — see what that does to the balance length.** With S unchanged, a larger X
needs a larger ratio ℓ/(100 − ℓ) ✓ That ratio increases with ℓ, so the balance point
must move **to the right**:
**the new balancing length is greater than ℓ** ✓
**Why the ratio increases with ℓ.** As ℓ grows, the numerator rises and the denominator
falls, so the fraction rises steeply ✓ At ℓ = 50 cm the ratio is 1; at 60 cm it is 1·5;
at 75 cm it is 3.
**A worked instance.** Suppose X = S initially, so ℓ = **50 cm**. Heating the coil by
enough to raise X by 20%:
X/S = 1·2 = ℓ/(100 − ℓ)
1·2(100 − ℓ) = ℓ
120 = 2·2ℓ
**ℓ = 54·5 cm** ✓ the balance point has moved 4·5 cm to the right.
**Why the water matters.** It is simply the means of heating the coil uniformly and
knowing its temperature ✓ The water's own conductivity plays no part, since the coil is
insulated.
**The physical reason metals behave this way.** Hotter lattice ions vibrate more, the
electrons' mean free time τ falls, and ρ = m/(ne²τ) rises ✓ A **semiconductor** would do
the opposite - its resistance falls with temperature - and the balance point would move
left.
**Reading the distractors.** **< ℓ** ✗ would need the coil's resistance to **fall**, as
in a thermistor. **= ℓ** ✗ would need no change at all. **= 0** ✗ would mean the coil's
resistance had dropped to zero ✓
∴ > l.
